fixes.explanation: Matthew says Herod heard the reports about Jesus (Matthew 14:1), and then Herod tells his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead! That is why miraculous powers are at work in him." (Matthew 14:2). Herod puts a name on it, and the name is John. He says it out loud to his servants, no hedging.

Elijah is a fair guess, baker, but it's not the name Herod says. Matthew records Herod telling his servants, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!…" (Matthew 14:2). Herod puts the miraculous powers down to John. Elijah never comes up in his words.

Jeremiah doesn't make it into Herod's mouth. What Herod says to his servants is, "This is John the Baptist; he has risen from the dead!…" (Matthew 14:2). He names one man, and it's John. Herod says it plainly.

Matthew tells us Herod had arrested John, bound him and put him in prison on account of Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, because John had been telling him, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:3-4). John's words were aimed right at Herod. The word John used is lawful.

I get why "safe" sounds right, because John ended up bound and in prison (Matthew 14:3). But John's words were about the law, not about safety. He said, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). I think that took real nerve, and the word he used is lawful.

"Wise" is a nice word, but it's not John's word. Matthew records him saying, "It is not lawful for you to have her." (Matthew 14:4). This was about Herod and Herodias, his brother Philip's wife (Matthew 14:3). The word John used is lawful.

Matthew says Herod had John bound and in prison (Matthew 14:3), and then adds, "Although Herod wanted to kill John, he was afraid of the people, because they regarded John as a prophet." (Matthew 14:5). Here's a ruler with a prison, and he's still watching the crowd. The text gives the reason right there: the people regarded John as a prophet.
The text says the opposite. The daughter of Herodias danced before them "…and pleased Herod…" (Matthew 14:6). Pleased is the word Matthew uses, and that matters for what happens next.

That's right, it's false. Matthew says the daughter of Herodias danced before them "…and pleased Herod…" (Matthew 14:6). The next verse shows how much: he promised with an oath to give her whatever she asked (Matthew 14:7). A pleased ruler on his birthday, and that's where the story turns.

Herod was so pleased that he "…promised with an oath to give to her whatever she asked." (Matthew 14:7). That's a blank check, signed with an oath. Later Matthew says Herod ordered her wish granted because of his oaths and his guests (Matthew 14:9).
Matthew says, "Prompted by her mother…" (Matthew 14:8). So the mother is the one who prompted her. The text tells us who, and it doesn't say how she did it.
It's true, not false. Matthew says, "Prompted by her mother…" (Matthew 14:8). Herodias is the one who prompted the girl. The text gives us the mother's part and doesn't say more than that.
